statement: A school club will sell exactly $80$ candles at a fair. Small candles sell for $\$6$ each and cost the club $\$1$ each to make. Large candles sell for $\$10$ each and cost the club $\$3$ each to make. What is the least number of large candles the club must sell to make a total profit of at least $\$500$?

choices.misconception: I used the selling prices as if they were all profit, so I solved $6(80 - L) + 10L \ge 500$, which gives $L \ge 5$.
I set up $5L + 7(80 - L) \ge 500$, giving the small-candle profit to the large candles, and got $L \le 30$, so I answered $30$.
I counted profit only from the large candles, so I solved $7L \ge 500$, got $L \ge 71.4$, and rounded up to $72$.

hints: Find the profit the club makes on one candle of each size.
Let $L$ be the number of large candles, so $80 - L$ are small. Write the total profit and require it to be at least $500$.

solutions.reliable: Each small candle earns $6 - 1 = 5$ dollars of profit, and each large candle earns $10 - 3 = 7$ dollars. With $L$ large candles and $80 - L$ small ones, the profit is $5(80 - L) + 7L = 400 + 2L$. We need $400 + 2L \ge 500$, so $2L \ge 100$ and $L \ge 50$. Check: $50$ large and $30$ small give $350 + 150 = 500$ dollars.
solutions.elegant: Selling all $80$ as small candles gives $80 \cdot 5 = 400$ dollars of profit. Each time a small candle is swapped for a large one the profit rises by $7 - 5 = 2$ dollars. The club needs $100$ dollars more, so it needs $100 \div 2 = 50$ swaps.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
